body.statement:
Suppose \(S_k=\{j\}\), where \(j\in\{k,k+1\}\cap\{1,\ldots,T\}\), and \(S_t=\varnothing\) for \(t\ne k\).  The finite procedure \(\mathsf A_1\) terminates after scanning \(\mathcal H(B)\).  If \(\mathcal H(B)\ne\varnothing\), it returns an evaluable rational map \(\mathsf{Rec}^{(1)}_{T,k,j,B}\) such that
\[
\mathsf{Rec}^{(1)}_{T,k,j,B}((M_d(P))_{d=0}^T)=Q(P)
\]
for every \(P\in\mathcal P_{T,S,B,e}\).  If \(\mathcal H(B)=\varnothing\), it returns two strictly positive laws \((P,P')=\mathsf{Wit}^{(1)}_{T,k,j,B}\) in \(\mathcal P_{T,S,B,e}\) with
\[
\Phi_{T,S,B,e}(P)=\Phi_{T,S,B,e}(P')
\quad\text{and}\quad Q(P)\ne Q(P').
\]
The construction is valid for every specified finite alphabet, every horizon \(T\), null effects on allowed arrows, and transition kernels of arbitrary rank.
body.proof_tex:
Fix the graph in the statement.  For notational clarity, condition temporarily on a cell \((W=w,A=a)\).  This cell and every dropout stratum have positive probability by \(\text{ass:substantive-positivity}\), \(\text{ass:hazard-positivity}\), and the factorization in \(\text{ass:substantive-markov}\).  Write \(q_t(w,a)=\gamma_t(w,a)\in(0,1)\) for \(t\ne k\); these hazards are constant in the substantive trajectory by \(\text{ass:local-hazards}\).

We first give the recovery branch.  All its ingredients are explicit functions of the pattern tables.  With \(I_T=\{1,\ldots,T\}\), define the stratum masses
\[
\tau_r(w,a)=\sum_{x_{I_r}}M_r(w,a,x_{I_r}),\qquad 0\le r\le T,
\tag{1}
\]
and recover
\[
p_W(w)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}\sum_{r=0}^T\tau_r(w,a).
\tag{2}
\]
If \(\ell\in B_d\), define the audited conditional marginal
\[
A_{d,\ell}(z\mid w,a)
=\frac{\displaystyle
\sum_{x_{I_d\setminus\{\ell\}}}M_d(w,a,x_{I_d})
}{\tau_d(w,a)}.
\tag{3}
\]
From complete cases define
\[
C_\ell(z\mid w,a)
=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{x_{1:T}:x_\ell=z}M_T(w,a,x_{1:T})}
{\tau_T(w,a)}
\tag{4}
\]
and
\[
L_{\ell,w,a}(x\mid z)
=\frac{\displaystyle
\sum_{x_{1:T}:x_\ell=z,\,x_T=x}M_T(w,a,x_{1:T})
}{\displaystyle
\sum_{x_{1:T}:x_\ell=z}M_T(w,a,x_{1:T})}.
\tag{5}
\]
When \(\ell=T\), (5) is the identity kernel.  Each denominator in (3)--(5) is strictly positive: every substantive trajectory has positive mass, every factor selecting its dropout stratum is positive, and the sums are finite and nonempty.

On \(D=T\), the conditional trajectory mass given \((w,a)\) is proportional to
\[
K_1(x_1\mid w,a)\prod_{t=2}^T K_t(x_t\mid w,a,x_{t-1})q_k(w,a,x_j),
\tag{6}
\]
because the remaining factors \(\prod_{t\ne k}\gamma_t(w,a)\) are constant.  For \(\ell\ge j\), condition on \(X_\ell=z\) in (6).  The sum of all factors through visit \(\ell\), including \(q_k(w,a,x_j)\), is then a common positive normalizing factor, whereas the suffix is
\[
\prod_{t=\ell+1}^T K_t(x_t\mid w,a,x_{t-1}).
\]
Normalization cancels the prefix factor.  Consequently
\[
L_{\ell,w,a}(x\mid z)
=\Pr(X_T=x\mid X_\ell=z,W=w,A=a).
\tag{7}
\]
This is a direct Markov-factorization calculation and uses no inversion or rank condition.

Let \((d,\ell)\) be the lexicographically first member of \(\mathcal H(B)\).  If \(d\le k-2\), the dropout event \(D=d\) has, conditional on \((w,a,X)\), the factor
\[
\left\{\prod_{s=1}^d\gamma_s(w,a)\right\}
\{1-\gamma_{d+1}(w,a)\},
\]
which does not depend on \(X\).  Hence
\[
\pi_{\ell,w,a}(z):=A_{d,\ell}(z\mid w,a)
=\Pr(X_\ell=z\mid W=w,A=a).
\tag{8}
\]

It remains to handle \(d=k-1\).  Define, using (1),
\[
\rho_{w,a}
=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{r=k}^T\tau_r(w,a)}
{\displaystyle\sum_{r=k-1}^T\tau_r(w,a)}
=\Pr(D\ge k\mid W=w,A=a,D\ge k-1).
\tag{9}
\]
The denominator is positive and \(0<\rho_{w,a}<1\) by hazard positivity.  The event \(D\ge k-1\) involves only the constants \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_{k-1}\), and is therefore independent of \(X\) given \((w,a)\).  Conditional on \(D\ge k\), all further continuation factors are constants, so the law of \(X_\ell\) is the same as its law conditional on \(D=T\), namely (4).  Partitioning \(D\ge k-1\) into \(D=k-1\) and \(D\ge k\) therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{\ell,w,a}(z)
&:=(1-\rho_{w,a})A_{k-1,\ell}(z\mid w,a)
+\rho_{w,a}C_\ell(z\mid w,a)\\
&=\Pr(X_\ell=z\mid W=w,A=a).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
Equations (2), (5), (8), and (10) define the returned map by
\[
\mathsf{Rec}^{(1)}_{T,k,j,B}((M_r)_{r=0}^T)_a(x)
=\sum_{w\in\mathcal W}p_W(w)
\sum_{z\in\mathcal X_\ell}
\pi_{\ell,w,a}(z)L_{\ell,w,a}(x\mid z).
\tag{11}
\]
Using (7) and the law of total probability in (11) yields
\[
\sum_w p_W(w)\Pr(X_T=x\mid W=w,A=a)
=Q_a(x),
\tag{12}
\]
where the last equality is the truncated substantive factorization in \(\text{def:causal-target}\).  Thus (11) is an observed-law functional whose equality to the causal target has been derived, not stipulated.  The calculation applies simultaneously to every \(a\) and \(x\), to null allowed-arrow effects, and to deficient transition ranks.

We now construct the obstruction branch.  Suppose \(\mathcal H(B)=\varnothing\).  Choose the first enumerated baseline cell \(w_\star\) and the first enumerated treatment cell \(a_\star\).  Keep a common strictly positive \(p_W\), a common strictly positive \(p_A\), and identical kernels and hazards outside this cell.  On every alphabet \(\mathcal X_r\), choose a strictly positive reference mass \(\nu_r\) and a nonconstant function \(h_r\) satisfying
\[
\sum_y\nu_r(y)h_r(y)=0,
\qquad |h_r(y)|\le1.
\tag{13}
\]
Such a pair exists because \(|\mathcal X_r|\ge2\): the procedure takes \(\nu_r\) uniform, assigns \(h_r=1\) and \(h_r=-1\) to the first two enumerated cells, and assigns zero to the rest.  It fixes \(\epsilon=1/2\), and on \(\mathcal X_j\) sets
\[
\mu(z)=\nu_j(z)\{1+\epsilon h_j(z)\},
\qquad
\mu'(z)=\nu_j(z)\{1-\epsilon h_j(z)\}.
\tag{14}
\]
Centering in (13) makes both vectors normalized; boundedness and \(\epsilon<1\) make them strictly positive.  They are distinct because \(h_j\) is nonconstant.  Put
\[
c(z)=\frac12\min\{\mu(z),\mu'(z)\},
\qquad
q_k(w_\star,a_\star,z)=\frac{c(z)}{\mu(z)},
\qquad
q'_k(w_\star,a_\star,z)=\frac{c(z)}{\mu'(z)}.
\tag{15}
\]
Then both hazards lie strictly between zero and one.  Take every other hazard to be a common constant in \((0,1)\).

Choose common positive kernels before visit \(j\), for example kernels that ignore their predecessor and have laws \(\nu_r\).  At \((w_\star,a_\star)\), let the visit-\(j\) kernel ignore its predecessor and equal \(\mu\) in the first model and \(\mu'\) in the second.  For \(r>j\), use in both models, with \(\lambda_r=1/2\),
\[
K_r(y\mid w_\star,a_\star,z)
=\nu_r(y)\{1+\lambda_r h_{r-1}(z)h_r(y)\},
\qquad \lambda_r=1/2.
\tag{16}
\]
Equation (13) shows that (16) sums to one in \(y\), and the bounds in (13) and \(\lambda_r<1\) show that every entry is strictly positive.  Moreover,
\[
\mathbb E\{h_r(X_r)\mid X_{r-1}=z,W=w_\star,A=a_\star\}
=\lambda_r h_{r-1}(z)\sigma_r^2,
\qquad
\sigma_r^2:=\sum_y\nu_r(y)h_r(y)^2>0.
\tag{17}
\]
At visit \(j\), (14) gives
\[
\mathbb E_\mu h_j-\mathbb E_{\mu'}h_j
=2\epsilon\sigma_j^2>0.
\tag{18}
\]
Iterating (17), the difference between the two interventional endpoint expectations of \(h_T\), conditional on \(w_\star\) and intervention \(A=a_\star\), is
\[
2\epsilon\sigma_j^2
\prod_{r=j+1}^T\lambda_r\sigma_r^2>0,
\tag{19}
\]
where an empty product is one.  All other baseline cells are common, so after averaging over \(W\) the difference is multiplied by \(p_W(w_\star)>0\).  Therefore the endpoint distributions differ in at least one cell, and hence \(Q(P)\ne Q(P')\).

It remains to verify equality of every observed table.  For every dropout index \(r\ge k\), the full subdensity is pointwise equal in the two models because the only changed substantive--response product is
\[
\mu(z)q_k(w_\star,a_\star,z)
=c(z)
=\mu'(z)q'_k(w_\star,a_\star,z).
\tag{20}
\]
Thus \(M_r=M'_r\) for \(r\ge k\).  If \(r\le k-2\), failure of \(\mathcal H(B)\) implies that every coordinate in \(I_r\) is smaller than \(j\).  The two models have the same law on those coordinates, and summing the normalized changed suffix from visit \(j\) onward gives one in both models.  Thus \(M_r=M'_r\).  Finally, every coordinate in \(I_{k-1}\) is also smaller than \(j\), while marginalizing the visit-\(j\) factor and the normalized downstream tail gives
\[
\sum_z\mu(z)\{1-q_k(w_\star,a_\star,z)\}
=1-\sum_zc(z)
=\sum_z\mu'(z)\{1-q'_k(w_\star,a_\star,z)\}.
\tag{21}
\]
Hence \(M_{k-1}=M'_{k-1}\) as well.  All other \((w,a)\) cells were held fixed.  The already-established \(\text{prop:audit-table-equivalence}\), using the same known \(e\), now gives
\[
\Phi_{T,S,B,e}(P)=\Phi_{T,S,B,e}(P').
\tag{22}
\]

Every substantive entry in the construction is positive by (13)--(16), and every hazard and failure probability is positive by (15) and the choice of the remaining constants.  Independent uniform disturbances, transformed by the inverse cumulative probabilities of the displayed finite kernels, realize these tables with mutually independent substantive and response noises.  Thus both laws lie in \(\mathcal P_{T,S,B,e}\) and respect the specified parent sets; ignored allowed parents are null effects.  The scan has only \(k(T-j+1)\) entries and the witness uses finitely many table entries, so \(\mathsf A_1\) terminates on both branches.  This proves the exhaustive single-hazard alternative.
